articles.summary: Maharashtra tightens regulation of dental labs, Check guidelines Medical Dialogues
articles.content: Mumbai: Taking note of the complaints regarding unqualified technicians and questionable materials used in dental aids, the Maharashtra Government has issued guidelines to regulate dental laboratories, technicians, manufacturers, and suppliers. In its resolution dated November 6, 2026, the State Government has also ordered inspections by the Food and Drug Administration to ensure compliance.Also Read: 18 Dentists, Doctors, Scientists Recognised in Stanford University's 2026 list of world's top 2% scientistsAccording to an Indian Express report, the Medical Education Department of Maharashtra has received more than 350 complaints since 2014, raising concerns regarding unqualified people undertaking dental laboratory work and the use of inferior materials. Commenting on this, Dr. Pallavi Saple, the Director of Medical Education and Research, said that this is mainly due to a shortage of trained personnel. Even though Maharashtra has around 66,000 registered dentists, there are only around 1,200 qualified dental technicians.Guidelines issued by the Maharashtra Government: In the order dated 06.11.2026, the Medical Education Department of Maharashtra mentioned that dentists take the assistance of dental technicians and dental laboratories for preparing artificial teeth, dentures, crowns, bridges, prosthetic structures on dental implants, appliances used for straightening teeth, and other restorative and dental appliances required for the oral healthcare treatment of patients.The Government clarified in the order that such work must be carried out according to the medical requirements of the patient, based on the examination conducted by the dentist and in accordance with the written or electronic instructions issued by the dentist.In the order, the Government pointed out that certain instances had come to notice where dental technicians accept work directly without written prescriptions or authorised instructions from dentists, prescribed technical standards are not followed, inferior-quality or unsuitable materials are used, necessary hygiene and sterilisation procedures are not followed, and essential records relating to the quality of work are not maintained.Highlighting that such practices may result in improper fabrication of artificial teeth and dental appliances, diseases affecting oral tissues, risk of infection, allergies, or other adverse effects. To protect the oral health of patients in Maharashtra and ensure that dental appliances are manufactured in accordance with the instructions of dentists, and to establish uniform procedures regarding minimum infrastructure, hygiene, sterilisation, quality of materials and record management for the functioning of dental technicians and dental laboratories, the Government has issued the following guidelines:Prescription by Dentist:(1) Artificial teeth, dentures, crowns, bridges, prosthetic structures on dental implants, appliances used for straightening teeth and other appliances manufactured by dental laboratories shall be fabricated only on the basis of written prescriptions or electronic instructions issued by a dentist.(2) The name and registration number of the dentist, the patient's reference number, the type of appliance, the material to be used, the shade and the necessary technical specifications must be mentioned on the prescription.(3) A dental technician shall not interfere in the scope of the dentist's medical diagnosis, treatment planning or treatment, and shall not accept work directly from patients.Manufacturing Licence:(4) All manufacturers in the State engaged in the fabrication/manufacture of dental appliances that are covered under the Medical Devices Rules, 2017 and classified as medical devices by CDSCO shall obtain the prescribed licence from the competent licensing authority, according to the risk classification of the device, before commencing manufacturing.(5) The risk classification of the device shall be determined according to the dental-device classification list notified by CDSCO. articles.title: Indian sports wrap, November 16: Mahimkar bags double at Bombay Gymkhana Maharashtra State Open Badminton - Sportstar
articles.summary: Indian sports wrap, November 16: Mahimkar bags double at Bombay Gymkhana Maharashtra State Open Badminton Sportstar
articles.content: Chennai BADMINTON Mahimkar bags double; Spruha, Anvisha win Greater Mumbai’s Harshit Mahimkar completed a notable double, claiming the men’s singles and boys under-19 singles titles at the Bombay Gymkhana presents Yonex Sunrise Bombay Gymkhana Maharashtra State Open Badminton Tournament. He then lived up to his status as the top seed in the boys under-19 category, beating Palghar’s 6th seed Ruturaj Chipat 15-9, 15-5. Unseeded Spruha Joshi of Mumbai Suburban, continuing her good form, showed nerve to recover from losing the first game and beat Greater Mumbai’s Anvisha Ghorpade 12-15, 15-6, 16-14 to win the girls under-19 title. Anvisha, however, had some consolation, as she won the under-17 final, beating Imaan Motorala 15-9, 15-7. All five individual events were in action on day one. In Mixed Doubles, Prince and Ishita Negi won 15-9, 13-15, 16-14 against Bhashy Pathak and Siona Gala, while Amith Raj Natraj and Suhina Roy beat Sanidhya Sunil Ekade and Yutika Chavan 15-9, 15-9. In Boys’ Singles, Arnav Yadav defeated Divyam Kejriwal 17-15, 15-5, and Vedansh Negi came from behind to beat Medhansh Sharma 7-15, 15-10, 15-6. Former champion Om Prakash Chouhan, Rashid Khan, Mohd Azhar, Akshay Sharma, Honey Baisoya and Manu Gandas lead the Indian challenge. The tournament is the longest-running on the Indian domestic circuit and on the DP World PGTI. -Team Sportstar MOTORSPORTS Formula E enters GEN4 era with new M13Electro Mahindra Racing today unveiled the M13Electro, its challenger for the 2027 Season of the ABB FIA Formula E World Championship. articles.title: India takes aim: The arrows, ambition and belief driving a new era in Indian archery - India Today
articles.summary: India takes aim: The arrows, ambition and belief driving a new era in Indian archery India Today
articles.content: South Korea has set the standard in international archery for decades. Its dominance, particularly in recurve, has been built on a system that continues to produce world-class athletes. India has had its moments against the Koreans, but building a team capable of challenging them regularly has been a different proposition altogether.Rahul Banerjee knows what that challenge looks like. A former Indian archer who competed at the Olympic and Commonwealth Games, Banerjee has experienced the demands of competing at the highest level. Now a coach, he is working with a generation of archers whose preparation looks very different from his own.In an exclusive interview with IndiaToday.in, Banerjee spoke about the changes in Indian archery, the growing confidence within the team and what it will take to turn that progress into an Olympic medal.Sports science, specialised strength and conditioning, video analysis and sports psychology have become part of the preparation. The Archery Premier League is also giving younger athletes opportunities to learn alongside established international names. But the biggest shift, Banerjee believes, is in the way India now approaches its strongest opponents.The gap with South Korea has not disappeared. Yet India's recent performances have given the team reason to believe it belongs among the contenders.His assessment is clear.“We are not underdogs anymore.”BREAKING THE BARRIERThere is a reason Banerjee is confident about India's standing. The 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya offered perhaps the clearest evidence yet, particularly in women's recurve.Ankita Bhakat, Kirti and Kumkum Mohod defeated South Korea 5-3 in the women's team final to win India's first-ever Asian Games gold in the event. The victory also ended a remarkable Korean run. South Korea had won every women's recurve team title at the Asian Games since 1998.Kumkum went a step further the following day. The 17-year-old beat South Korea's Oh Yejin in a shoot-off to win the individual recurve gold, becoming the first Indian archer to claim that title at the Asian Games. She had also beaten Korean world champion Kang Chaeyoung in the quarter-finals.The men's recurve team, however, lost 5-1 to South Korea in the final. The result was a reminder that India has not closed the gap across every event. Korea remains a formidable opponent, backed by a system that produces technically accomplished archers across generations.Banerjee believes the younger Indian archers are beginning to approach these contests differently. He recalled speaking to Kumkum about her mindset during the Asian Games. Her response stayed with him.“Humne kuch socha hi nahi, main toh gaya aur chalaya (I did not think about anything, I just went and shot),” he recalled her saying.She had not allowed the occasion or the reputation of her opponent to dominate her thinking. She went out and focused on shooting.“Pressure is for everyone,” Banerjee said. Producing a 10 in a decisive moment, he explained, comes down to practice and knowing when to execute the shot.He is careful not to mistake a few landmark victories for a complete shift in the sport's hierarchy. South Korea's advantage comes from the depth of its programme. Its archers move through a structured pathway that begins in schools and continues through universities and corporate teams. Making the national team is an achievement in itself.The coach sees a similar level of competition emerging in India's compound programme. He estimates that around 60 Indian compound archers can shoot 700 out of 720, creating intense competition for places in the national squad. Recurve still needs to develop that kind of depth, among both men and women.“That thing we need to bring into Indian recurve,” he said. “We have to have more athletes with better technique.”India has beaten South Korea on major occasions. Banerjee's ambition, however, goes beyond producing another upset. He wants enough Indian archers capable of challenging the Koreans consistently, rather than depending on a small group of leading performers.THE SCIENCE SHIFTFor Banerjee, India's progress cannot be separated from the way its archers are now trained. The difference between his generation and the current one is the support available around the athlete, particularly in physical conditioning and mental preparation.“When we were competing, sports science was not introduced,” he said. “I came to know about physiotherapy, manual therapy and started working with sports psychology in the middle of my career.”Training in those days was largely built around repetition and general fitness. Archers were expected to put in the hours, shoot more arrows and work on their strength through conventional weight training. Specialised support was not part of their everyday routine.The approach has changed. At the academy where Banerjee works, psychologists begin working with archers when they are around 15 or 16. Young athletes are introduced to meditation and visualisation, while strength trainers focus on the specific muscle groups used in archery.“Nowadays, we have proper strength trainers who know which muscles we need to use,” he said. “We have psychology, they suggest what kind of visualisation we need to do.”Banerjee has also seen technology change the way coaches assess technique. He says his academy was among the first in India to introduce Dartfish video analysis, allowing coaches to study an athlete's movements and identify areas that need attention. Korean archers, he says, had been using similar technology for around 15 years before it became more common in India.He believes the impact can be seen in the depth of the domestic pool. During his competitive years, he recalls, only three or four Indian archers could produce the scores now reached by the country's leading athletes. Today, he estimates that around 16 can reach that level.“Now the bench strength of Indian archery has increased,” he said, pointing to the growth of academies, support systems and sports science.Banerjee also credits government programmes and private organisations, including the Reliance Foundation, with supporting athletes. The exchange of knowledge between Indian and overseas coaches has added another dimension to their preparation.“During our time, we were used to generalised training. We had to work hard, shoot more arrows,” he said. “Now there are multiple academies, multiple support systems.”THE MIND GAMEAn archer can spend years perfecting technique and developing the consistency to shoot high scores. None of that guarantees the same performance when an Olympic medal is on the line. Banerjee knows this from experience. He says the pressure of a major final can change the way an archer physically experiences a shot.One problem, he explains, is that the bow can suddenly feel lighter than it actually is. An archer accustomed to drawing 50 pounds may feel as though the bow has dropped to 30 pounds when the pressure becomes intense. That altered sensation can affect the release, producing what Banerjee describes as a loose shot.“Archery is a sport of feeling,” he said. “When you're in too much pressure, you'll feel like you're drawing 30 pounds.”His approach begins with breathing. Young archers at his academy are taught stomach breathing and encouraged to spend five to 10 minutes visualising their performance before a match. The aim is to bring their attention back to the task before they step onto the shooting line.Every archer has an individual sequence. One might focus on the position of the left hand, another on breathing, the hook or the movement of the drawing elbow. The details differ, but the purpose is the same: to give the mind something familiar to follow when the pressure rises.“Your work is to shoot according to your shooting form,” Banerjee said. “If you're focusing on the opponent, that he has shot a 10 and I have to shoot a 10, things become worse.”Archery, he stresses, is a contest in which the athlete must concentrate on executing a shot rather than reacting to an opponent's next move. Watching the opponent's score can pull attention away from the technique.Banerjee uses the example of driving a manual car. Once a person has repeated the movements enough times, changing gears and coordinating the pedals become instinctive. Under pressure, an archer needs a similar level of familiarity with the shooting sequence.“Even if you're talking to someone while driving, you can easily drive because your mind and body are coordinated,” he explained. “The same process you are following in a sport like archery.”The conditions outside an archer's control add another layer. Wind can push the athlete's aim from side to side and alter the arrow's trajectory. Archers must read the wind flags and windsocks around the field, then make adjustments based on experience.Physical strength and equipment choices also influence how an archer deals with wind. A higher draw weight can give an arrow greater speed, reducing the extent to which wind affects its flight. But that comes with a physical demand, particularly in recurve, where the archer must hold the draw weight throughout the shot.For Banerjee, technique, physical preparation and mental control are connected. An athlete cannot depend on one of them alone when a match reaches its decisive moments.THE APL EFFECTThe Archery Premier League has introduced a different kind of pressure. At a regular World Archery event, competitors have 20 seconds to shoot an arrow. The APL cuts that down to 15. With compound and recurve archers competing together, teams must complete eight arrows in two minutes.The shorter window is particularly demanding for compound archers, who have to account for their sight, aim, wind conditions and reflections on their lenses. Team coordination becomes just as important. If one archer takes longer than expected, the others have to adjust.Banerjee believes the format has also helped archers spend less time thinking about the pressure itself. With so little time available, there is limited room to overanalyse a shot.He spoke to several archers after close finishes in the league, including competitors who had to produce a 10 with only seconds remaining. Their responses were remarkably similar.“Nothing was going on in my mind. I just need to finish the arrow. I just need to aim and follow my process,” he recalled them saying.The effect has been noticeable among younger Indian archers. Banerjee remembered a conversation he had with a youngster after a national competition in Jaipur. She told him that she had been shooting within nine seconds and had twice stepped away from the line before her coach reminded her that this was not the APL and she had time to complete her shot.The league's influence extends beyond its faster format. Sharing a team with established international competitors gives young archers an opportunity to learn from people they have previously watched from a distance.That exchange is what Banerjee believes the league was designed to encourage. Indian archers can observe how leading international athletes train and prepare, while also having the chance to ask questions directly.The exchange works both ways. Banerjee recalled Nico (Weiner) of the Kakatiya Knights asking him to give one of his Indian teammates an opportunity to compete, despite being one of the team's leading archers himself. The message was about putting the team first: win or lose, the team does it together.Even international competitors have found value in the experience.For Banerjee, this exchange of knowledge is one of the APL's most important contributions. It gives Indian archers access to expertise that might otherwise take years to encounter, while making them more comfortable around athletes they once considered distant role models.THE OLYMPIC TESTFor all the progress Indian archery has made, the biggest test still lies ahead. articles.title: Prince William, Princess Kate get taste of Mumbai street food with Sachin Tendulkar - India Today
articles.summary: Prince William, Princess Kate get taste of Mumbai street food with Sachin Tendulkar India Today
articles.content: Prince William and Princess Kate had a familiar face for company as they explored the streets of Mumbai, with cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar joining the royal couple for a walk through the city. The trio were spotted together outside Hamilton Studios, one of India's oldest photography studios, before taking in some of Mumbai's street food, including a cutting chai, and local flavour.The meeting brought together Britain's future king and queen with one of India's most celebrated sporting icons. William and Kate arrived in Mumbai on Monday for a three-day visit to India, with Tendulkar among the prominent personalities expected to be part of their engagements in the city. The royal couple were seen walking alongside Tendulkar through Ballard Estate, getting a glimpse of Mumbai beyond its usual tourist attractions. The visit also included a taste of the city's street food, adding a relaxed, informal touch to an otherwise high-profile trip.And, inevitably, there was cricket. Kate later tried her hand at gully cricket, taking a few swings as children stationed close to the batter waited to catch the ball.But both Kate and William lost their wickets, prompting the Princess of Wales to admit with a smile: "I think we need some more practice, so next time!"The couple's cricket connection with Mumbai dates back to April 2016, when they played street cricket with local children during their first official visit to India. A decade later, the city has brought them back to the game, this time with Tendulkar, one of its most celebrated sporting icons, alongside them. William and Kate's Mumbai engagements extend beyond sport, with the couple also expected to take a ride on the city's Metro rail and interact with personalities from Bollywood. They will attend the Earthshot Prize ceremony on Tuesday before travelling to New Delhi, where they are scheduled to meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday.WHY ARE PRINCE WILLIAM AND PRINCESS KATE IN MUMBAI?The Prince and Princess of Wales are in India for the sixth edition of the Earthshot Prize, an environmental initiative founded by William in 2020 to identify and support innovative solutions to the planet's biggest challenges. Five winners will receive Â£1 million each to scale up their projects, with this year's ceremony being the biggest edition of the awards so far.The Mumbai programme will highlight the longstanding cultural connections between India and the UK through cricket, fashion and cinema. Bollywood personalities, including Alia Bhatt, are among those expected at the awards ceremony, while British pop group Take That are also scheduled to perform.The visit is particularly significant for Kate, marking her most high-profile overseas engagement since undergoing preventative chemotherapy in 2024. The couple's previous official visit to India was in April 2016, when they also travelled to Bhutan.Beyond the awards, the visit is intended to highlight growing cooperation between India and the UK in clean energy, sustainable transport, innovation and trade. Their final engagement will be a meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi, bringing the three-day visit to a close.- Ends

articles.content: CHENNAI BADMINTON Karnataka boys, Tamil Nadu girls crowned champions in 49th Junior Team Championships Karnataka boys and Tamil Nadu girls were crowned champions in the 49th Junior National Badminton Championships with comfortable 2-0 wins over their respective opponents. With both defending champions Mizoram boys and Telangana girls failing to qualify for the Inter-Zonals, the titles were up for grabs. In the finals, Karnataka defeated Assam 2-0 while Tamil Nadu girls got the better of last edition silver medallist Delhi 2-0. In the girls’ team final, 2025 Asian Under-17 girls singles champion Diksha SR gave Tamil Nadu a winning start as she defeated Rishika Nandi 15-12, 15-12. The women’s doubles combination of Ananya Arun and Anjana Manikandan then sealed the victory with a 16-14, 12-15, 15-10 lead over Nandi and Ishita Negi. The men’s singles final saw Hardik Divyansh defeat 2023 Asian U-15 champion Bornil Changmai. The formidable combination of Pavan and Punith Suresh then got the better of Changmai and Aanayan Borah 9-15, 15-10, 7-15 to clinch the crown. RESULTS Boys U-19: Karnataka bt Assam 2-0 (Hardik Divyansh bt Bornil Changmai 18-16, 15-6; Pavan Suresh/Punith Suresh bt Aanayan Borah/Changmai 15-9, 10-15, 15-7) Girls U-19: Tamil Nadu bt Delhi 2-0 (Diksha SR bt Rishika Nandi 15-12, 15-12; Ananya Arun/Anjana Manikandan bt Nandi/Ishita Negi 16-14, 12-15, 15-10) -Team Sportstar MOTORSPORTS Dramatic opening day of National Car Racing Championship The opening day of round 2 of the CTR-JK Tyre FMSCI Indian National Car Racing Championship was dramatic in nature, filled with late changes and overtakes. Augustine Boby edged Shatveer Shetty by a mere 0.032 seconds in the F1300 Novice Cup here on Sunday. Mehul Agarwal produced a late overtake to beat teammate Arya Singh by 0.237 seconds in LGB Formula 4, while Deepak Ravikumar staged a remarkable recovery from 15th after an early stall to win the second Indian Junior Touring Cars race by 0.308 seconds. Srinivas Teja had won the opening race in the category. In the other categories, Bengaluru’s Anish Shetty won the Royal Enfield Continental GT Cup Pro race, while Vadodara’s Kabir Sahoch continued his winning run in the amateur class despite two red-flag interruptions at the Kari Motor Speedway. Mumbai’s Pratik Sonawane completed a double in the gentleman class of the JK Tyre Levitas Cup, while Arjun Narendran won the Indian Super Touring Cars race and Balaprasath A triumphed in Indian Touring Cars. Diljith T S also secured a double in Super Stock. The Royal Enfield Continental GT Cup amateur race witnessed further drama with a last-lap collision between Paramjeet Singh and Pushpendra Kumar Markandey, allowing Brandon Dsouza to climb from ninth on the grid to third. Action concludes on Sunday with the final day of round 2. -Team Sportstar MORE SPORTS Six cities across Telangana to host the Khelo India Youth Games 2026 The logo and mascot for the eighth edition of Khelo India Youth Games were unveiled on Sunday by Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya and Telangana Chief Minister A Revanath Reddy. The tournament is going to be played across six cities in Telangana: Hyderabad, Khammam, Karimnagar, Hanumakonda, Mahabubnagar and Nizamabad, between December 11 and 22. Around 8000 athletes are expected to participate in the event. “The Union Government, under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, is committed to promoting sports. Various competitions, including the Khelo India Youth Games, Beach Games, Winter Games and Tribal Games, are being organised under the Khelo India initiative to encourage greater participation of the younger generation in sports,” said Mandaviya. This time, the tournament will have 29 events, including two demonstration events: sailing and karra samu. Softball will also make its debut as a competitive sport in the tournament. -Team Sportstar With inputs from PTI CHESS Final day of Maharashtra State Schools Chess Championship 2026 Veer Dhaval Shah and AIM Hriday Maniar produced outstanding performances, winning all seven games in their respective categories, as the Maharashtra State Schools Chess Championship 2026 concluded at Rustomjee Cambridge International School, Dahisar (West), on Sunday. The three-day championship, organised by Indian Chess School, witnessed keen competition among 387 players across six FIDE-rated categories in the Under-9, Under-13 and Under-17 Open and Girls sections. In the Under-9 Open category, Veer Dhaval Shah (1501) of Jamnabai Narsee School, JVPD, emerged as the undisputed champion with a perfect score of seven points from seven rounds. Ivaan Dubey (1545), who had earlier won the Under-7 Open title in the first stage, secured second place with six points, while Aarav Ravi Jhavar (1571) of Jamnabai Narsee School finished third with six points. The Under-9 Girls category witnessed an exciting three-way finish, with Lavanya Singh (1448) of Sanjivani International School emerging champion with six points on superior tie-break. Ishi Singh (1538) of J. B. Petit High School for Girls also scored six points to secure second place, while Nikita Sandeep (1411) finished third with six points. In the Under-13 Open category, Vihaan Anupam Agrawal (1858) of Narayana Olympiad School emerged champion with six points from seven rounds, edging out top seed Nirvaan Nirav Shah (1956) of Don Bosco International School, who also scored six points but had to settle for second place on tie-break. In the Under-13 Girls category, Tisyaa Apurva Patt (1524) of Avalon Heights International School produced an impressive performance to clinch the championship with six points from seven rounds. Pranitha Bhava (1655) of Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan Vidyalaya secured second place with 5.5 points. The Under-17 Open category witnessed a commanding performance by top seed AIM Hriday Maniar (1910), who maintained his winning streak throughout the championship to secure the title with a perfect score of seven points from seven rounds. Shaurya Ashish Modi (1626) finished second with 5.5 points, while Soham Sudarshan Sahamate (1667) secured third place, also with 5.5 points. In the Under-17 Girls category, top seed Drishya Naik (1713) emerged as a convincing champion with 6.5 points from seven rounds, finishing 1.5 points ahead of her nearest challengers. The championship served as the selection tournament for the National Schools Chess Championship, scheduled to be held in Ahmedabad from December 16 to 20, 2026. The top two finishers in each of the six categories have earned the opportunity to represent Maharashtra at the national championship. -Team Sportstar RESULTS Boys U-19: Karnataka bt Assam 2-0 (Hardik Divyansh bt Bornil Changmai 18-16, 15-6; Pavan Suresh/Punith Suresh bt Aanayan Borah/Changmai 15-9, 10-15, 15-7) Girls U-19: Tamil Nadu bt Delhi 2-0 (Diksha SR bt Rishika Nandi 15-12, 15-12; Ananya Arun/Anjana Manikandan bt Nandi/Ishita Negi 16-14, 12-15, 15-10)

articles.summary: Maharashtra government urges drought-hit farmers to complete e-KYC, obtain Farmer IDs to access benefits The Hindu
articles.content: Mumbai The Maharashtra government’s Relief and Rehabilitation Department on Saturday (November 14) urged drought-affected farmers across the State to complete their e-KYC verification and obtain Farmer IDs at the earliest to ensure they can access financial assistance and benefits under various Central and State government schemes. Also read | Drought-stricken Beed: Land of parched fields and broken promises https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/maharashtra/drought-stricken-beed-land-of-parched-fields-and-broken-promises/article71689837.ece The appeal comes in the wake of the State government’s decision to provide advance financial assistance to drought-affected farmers before Diwali. According to the department, completing the necessary registration and verification procedures is essential for eligible beneficiaries to receive funds directly in their bank accounts. In a statement, the department said farmers must ensure that their information is updated on the AgriStack platform, which maintains updated farmer information and facilitates the delivery of benefits under agricultural and other government welfare schemes. It added that completing e-KYC verification and obtaining a Farmer ID would help minimise difficulties in accessing assistance and facilitate the timely transfer of benefits to eligible farmers. The State government also assured farmers that necessary assistance would be provided to resolve technical or other difficulties encountered during registration and verification. Farmers facing such issues have been advised to contact the relevant authorities rather than leave their applications incomplete. To obtain a Farmer ID, farmers have been asked to visit their nearest Common Service Centre (CSC) with their Aadhaar card and Aadhaar-linked mobile number to complete the registration process. The department reiterated that updating farmer records and completing verification procedures were important to ensure the timely and transparent distribution of government benefits. It urged farmers across Maharashtra, particularly those affected by drought, to prioritise the process and complete the required formalities without delay.
